evoke.e: From French évoquer, from Latin ēvocō (“to call out, summon”), from ex (“out”) and vocō (“call”). Akin to voice.

s.d: call forth (emotions, feelings, and responses)
x: arouse pity
raise a smile

s.d: evoke or provoke to appear or occur
x: Her behavior provoked a quarrel between the couple

s.d: deduce (a principle) or construe (a meaning)
x: We drew out some interesting linguistic data from the native informant

s.d: summon into action or bring into existence, often as if by magic
x: raise the specter of unemployment
he conjured wild birds in the air

s.d: call to mind
x: These pictures bring back sad memories
this remark evoked sadness

s.d: To call out; to draw out or bring forth.
To cause the manifestation of something (emotion, picture, etc.) in someone's mind or imagination.
x: Being here evokes long forgotten memories.
Seeing this happen equally evokes fear and anger in me.

s.d: To elicit a response.
called forth from a latent or potential state by stimulation
x: evoked potentials
an elicited response

s.d: the electrical response of the central nervous system produced by an external stimulus
x: he measured evoked potentials with an electroencephalogram

s.d: An electrical potential recorded from a human or animal following presentation of a stimulus, as distinct from spontaneous potentials as detected by electroencephalograms or electromyograms.

evolution.e:
Borrowed from Latin ēvolūtiō, ēvolūtiōnis (“the act of unrolling, unfolding or opening (of a book)”), from ēvolūtus, perfect passive participle of ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ex + volvō (“roll”).
Compare typologically Czech vývoj, Serbo-Croatian развој, Russian разви́ть (razvítʹ), развива́ть (razvivátʹ), разви́ться (razvítʹsja), развива́ться (razvivátʹsja), Russian разви́тие (razvítije), related to Proto-Slavic *viti (whence Czech vít, Russian вить (vitʹ)).

s.d: a process in which something passes by degrees to a different stage (especially a more advanced or mature stage)
x: the development of his ideas took many years
the evolution of Greek civilization

s.d: (biology) the sequence of events involved in the evolutionary development of a species or taxonomic group of organisms
(uncountable) A change of position.: A manoeuvre of troops or ships.
x: Mean while, he never failed to be present, when any regiment, or corps of men, were drawn out to be exercised and reviewed, and accompanied them in all their evolutions […].
Major Holroyd, who acted as the General, was extremely polite, and attentive, and came to us between every evolution, to explain and talk over the manoeuvres.

s.d: (uncountable) A change of position.: A turning movement, especially of the body.
x: It was a critical instant: the pirouette -- it would fail, she feared. … the rapid whirl achieved in exact time, the whole evolution executed to perfection.
"Look now, that pirouette -- my stars! how Beauchamp would stare to see his darling perform such an evolution!"

s.d: (obsolete, uncountable) A change of position.: A turned or twisted shape; an involution, a complex or intricate shape.
x: ‘It is not in the showy evolutions of buildings, but in the multiplicity of human habitations which are crouded together, that the wonderful immensity of London consists.’

s.d: (archaic, uncountable) An unfolding.: The act or process of unfolding or opening out; the progression of events in regular succession.
x: The world […] might have been gradually produced from very small beginnings […] rather than by a sudden evolution of the whole by the Almighty fiat.

s.d: (uncountable) An unfolding.: The opening out of a curve; now more generally, the gradual transformation of a curve by a change of the conditions generating it.
(historical, uncountable) An unfolding.: The extraction of a root from a given power.
(uncountable) An unfolding.: The act or an instance of giving off gas; emission.
x: Allantoxaidin is decomposed on heating, with evolution of ammonia and cyanic acid.

s.d: (uncountable) Process of development.: Development; the act or result of developing what was implicit in an idea, argument etc.
x: The ongoing evolution of Lolita subculture fashion includes, among other things, the ballet style.
Suffering has a noble purpose: the evolution of consciousness and the burning up of the ego.

s.d: (uncountable) Process of development.: A process of gradual change in a given system, subject, product etc., especially from simpler to more complex forms.
x: Among other forms of change, the evolution of transportation has involved modification, diversification, convergence, divergence, hybridization, differentiation, and naturally, selection.
There are some examples of cultural evolution in birds and monkeys, but […] it is our own species that really shows what cultural evolution can do.

s.d: (uncountable) Process of development.: The transformation of animals, plants and other living things into different forms (now understood as a change in genetic composition) by the accumulation of changes over successive generations.
x: [Some books have] made the erroneous assumption that the important thing in evolution is the good of the species (or the group) rather than the good of the individual (or the gene).

Many genes with reproductive roles also have antibacterial and immune functions, which indicate that the threat of microbial attack on the sperm or egg may be a major influence on rapid evolution during reproduction.

A proponent or supporter of evolutionism.
x: Ironically, the argument used today by Roadruck and other designists—that their teachings should receive equal time in schools—mirrors the one employed by evolutionists some 75 years ago.

s.d: Someone who believes in the capacity of people to change.
x: Aeschylus is in fact an evolutionist as regards both gods and man.

evolve.e: Borrowed from Latin ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē- (“out of”) (short form of ex) + volvō (“roll”).

s.d: work out
x: We have developed a new theory of evolution

s.d: undergo development or evolution
x: Modern man evolved a long time ago

s.d: gain through experience
x: I acquired a strong aversion to television
Children must develop a sense of right and wrong

s.d: To move (something) in regular procession through a system.
x: The animal soul sooner expands and evolves it self to its full orb and extent than the humane Soul

s.d: To change or transform (something).
x: Over several years the author evolved the story originally drafted as a novella into a real epic.

s.d: To cause (something) to come into being or develop.
x: You will remove the pig, place it in the car, and drive it to my house in Wiltshire. That is the plan I have evolved.
The interpreter has spent a whole lot of time working the music before the performance, trying to evolve the most accurate translation possible.

s.d: To acquire or develop (a trait) in the process of biological evolution.
x: How long ago did birds evolve beaks?

Oxygen levels on Earth skyrocketed 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis: the ability to convert water and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and waste oxygen using solar energy.

s.d: To change genetic composition over successive generations through the process of evolution.
x: A hundred thousand years from now, will Homo sapiens have evolved into beings unrecognizable to their ancestors?
I like to envision a species of humanoids that, having evolved on the moon with one-sixth earth's gravity, are double our height but too spindly to play basketball.

s.d: To give off (a gas such as carbon dioxide or oxygen) during a chemical reaction.
x: to evolve odours

s.d: (obsolete) To wind or unwind (something).
x: And come, my Muſe! that lov'ſt the ſylvan ſhade, / Evolve the mazes, and the miſt diſpel; / Tranſlate the ſong; convince my doubting maid / No ſolemn Derviſe can explain ſo vvell— […]

s.d: Of a trait; to develop within a population through biological evolution.
x: How long ago did beaks evolve?
